The architects for both these monuments purposefully designed them to be observation points for visitors in addition to being memorials. Already positioned on natural hills, the additional height of the two monument towers provides some of the best views of the entire City of Boston as well as Boston Harbor. To provide greater access to these views, NPS staff installed and began operating webcams from these monuments in 2020. Each monument has four cameras—one for each cardinal direction—and update approximately every minute. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Weeds and Invasives The BLM manages 245 million acres of public lands primarily in the Western United States, including Alaska. Seventy-nine million of these acres are impacted by noxious and invasive weeds. One of the BLM's highest priorities is to promote ecosystem health and one of the greatest obstacles to achieving this goal is the rapid expansion of weeds across public lands. These invasive plants can dominate and often cause permanent damage to natural plant communities. If not eradicated or controlled, noxious weeds will continue to jeopardize the health of the public lands and to constrain the myriad activities that occur on public lands. About Weeds and Invasives The term "weed" means different things to different people. In the broadest sense, it is any plant growing where it is not wanted. Weeds can be native or non-native, invasive or non invasive, and noxious or not noxious. Learn more and review Frequently Asked Questions . Set yourself up for success If you're like many people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, weight loss is part of your treatment plan. It sounds so simple: eat less and move more. But if weight loss were that easy, millions of people wouldn't be struggling right now to do it. And you've probably noticed that even people who take the weight off have a hard time keeping it off. More and more studies show that people respond differently to diets. For example, some lose weight on low carb; some gain weight. The same goes for other plans. This excerpt from the Baseball Traveler newsletter, presented by Circle K, is a mere taste of the smorgasbord of delights he offers every week. Read the full newsletter here , and subscribe to his newsletter here . They took the field in those jerseys?! No corner of the sports world has prompted this incredulous query more than Minor League Baseball, whose teams regularly wear outlandish theme jerseys in addition to their regular uniforms. To be a Minor League fan is to be exposed, on a daily basis, to a cornucopia of bold colors and bolder design. Check out jerseys in the MiLB Shop Ten examples of some of the boldest –- and probably the weirdest -- can be found below, all of which debuted during the era of sartorial excess that was the 2010s. Let's take a trip down memory lane, marveling anew at these groundbreaking and bizarre Minor League jerseys. (Note: Teams are listed at their current affiliation and level of play, which may have changed since the time these jerseys were first worn.) Bacon-themed uniforms (Lehigh Valley IronPigs, Triple-A PHI, 2014) Like Dylan going electric in 1965, the IronPigs' bacon-themed duds were an epochal event that firmly delineated the start of a new era. These uniforms, featuring bacon-strip hats and jerseys with a strip of bacon underneath a "'Pigs" wordmark, planted the seed for the food-themed alternate identity craze that continues in the Minor Leagues to this day. At the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), we work to increase success for people with disabilities in America's workplaces. This is a goal we share with our Alliance partner the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society (PBATS). Over the years, ODEP and PBATS have collaborated on a number of activities, including the production of several public service announcements (PSAs) featuring former MLB players with disabilities and/or professional baseball athletic trainers from clubs around the country. Among the topics these PSAs address is the importance of helping people stay at or return to work after injury or illness and, most recently, strategies for fostering mental health-friendly workplaces. Please view and share these PSAs and explore our resources for fostering supportive workplaces, for all workers in all types of workplaces—because everyone should be in the game. Wellbore Construction and Evaluation Wellbores are a critical component of the infrastructure and success of geothermal electricity generation projects and represent a significant hurdle for developers. Improving the durability and costs of wellbore structures and ensuring long-term well flow are vital to reduce costs and ensure safe, efficient operation of geothermal power plants. The Office of Geothermal is funding projects that can support these needs for both next-generation and conventional geothermal systems. By improving ways to build, assess, and maintain geothermal wellbores, these projects will expand opportunities to tap firm, flexible, domestic geothermal energy nationwide. Wells of Opportunity A key step to unlocking the full potential of reliable, domestic geothermal energy may lie inside millions of American oil and gas wells . These wells can be used to harness geothermal energy in two ways: through the retrofitting of inactive or unproductive wells, or through co-production on active wells. Well Retrofits In well retrofits, an unused, dry, or unproductive oil and gas well first undergoes any repairs necessary for safe operation. Water is then pumped into the oil and gas well, where it is warmed by the earth and drawn back to the surface to power a thermoelectric generator. The hot water pulled to the surface can be used for heating, cooling, or to power nearby structures and homes. America has millions of dry or unproductive oil and gas wells, many of which could be retrofitted for geothermal use. Note: The scope of the Office of Geothermal’s WOO initiative specifically targets inactive or unproductive wells. Daynes/Science Photo Library By Annie Roth Published February 26, 2026 Neanderthal men may have had a thing for modern human women, or perhaps Neanderthal men had something human women couldn't resist. That’s one potential interpretation of a new study, published Thursday in Science , that found when Neanderthals and Homo sapiens interbred, the pairings were predominantly between Neanderthal men and human women. Scientists have long known that some of our ancestors reproduced with Neanderthals before the species went extinct roughly 40,000 years ago. Today, traces of Neanderthal DNA linger in the genomes of many people, particularly among those with non-African ancestry. On average, it amounts to about one to two percent of a person’s genome. pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom. At dawn of a two-week lunar day, Edwin Aldrin strides across a small crater near one of Eagle's foil-wrapped landing probes. Visor reflects his long black shadow, the solar wind collector, the Stars and Stripes planted by the moonwalkers, the white figure of Armstrong (who took this picture), and the buglike lunar module. A renowned statistician, he’d retired from his teaching post at the University of California Berkeley. “We thought it was anxiety or depression,” says his daughter, Liz Selvin.
